newsitem.title: DUBAI: UAE central bank governor sees one pct real growth.
newsitem.headline: UAE central bank governor sees one pct real growth.

text.p: The governor of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) Central Bank Sultan bin Nasser al-Suweidi said he expected the economy to grow this year at around, or slightly below, the real rate of one percent seen last year.

"The UAE economy grew by approximately one percent in real terms last year. Given events that have recently impacted on our economy, I believe that we may experience a similar to slightly lower rate of real growth during 1996 and 1997," he said in a speech to businessmen earlier this week.
The text of his address was obtained by Reuters on Thursday.
"These are a slight downward revision to figures that I would have forecast six months ago," he said.
Suweidi said the "continued and unexpected firming" of oil prices this year would lead to a slight increase in oil's contribution to GDP.

"Going forward, however, these price levels cannot be sustained. Therefore, assuming a softening in oil prices and unchanged OPEC production levels, I would expect a reversal of this positive (increasing) contribution to GDP," he said.
A string of new infrastructure and industrial projects would benefit exports and the economy in the longer run.
But in the short-term, Suweidi said there would be a small impact on the economy of a crackdown on illegal aliens.
About 200,000 people have left the Gulf state in recent weeks to avoid tough new penalties for working illegally.
"Unfortunately, an unintended, yet indirect, impact of this improved social environment may be a temporary slowdown in some labour intensive businesses."
"As such, some construction and agricultural businesses may be squeezed until replacement workers are hired," he said.
But longer-term the social environment would improve and tourism could benefit.

Referring to the banking sector, Suweidi said an improved financial disclosure regime would be finalised and announced soon. "This disclosure will better enable large and small depositors to better assess their choice of where to place their savings. It shall also bring market forces to bear on bankers to manage their institutions properly."
